b: The Spagitty wiki Spagitty Untangle the work — yours, and your agents'. Spagitty is a local-first desktop Git client for repositories where people and coding agents commit side by side — and it is where those agents are run : a goal, the tasks it was cut into, and the agents already installed on your machine working them in parallel, each on its own branch, in its own worktree. Download the latest release What Spagitty is The agent farm Version 0.5.1 Linux · macOS · Windows Tauri 2 Rust 1.77+ Svelte 5 / SvelteKit 2 gitoxide (gix) GPL-3.0-or-later No telemetry This wiki is the complete documentation for Spagitty: what it does, how each screen works, how the code is arranged, and how we build and release it. It is written for three readers — someone deciding whether to use Spagitty, someone using it and looking for a specific thing, and someone reading or changing the source. Start here Orientation What Spagitty is The problem it solves, the principles behind it, and what it deliberately is not. Get running Install & first run Grab a build for your platform, open a repository, or build from source. Reference Feature reference Everything Spagitty ships, grouped by what you are trying to do. The headline The agent farm A goal, a plan, and four agents working it in parallel under rules they cannot skip. Reference Screens 1A–1Q Every screen by its code, what it is for, and what it deliberately does not do. Under the hood Architecture Three layers, two boundaries, and the seams that keep them honest. What it looks like 1A The graph — a streamed, virtualised commit list with a lane canvas, author portraits generated locally from each email, and almost every operation Spagitty can perform one right-click away. Spagitty in one page It is a Git client first The commit graph, the working copy, diffs, branches, stashes, tags, the reflog, file history and blame, interactive rebase, conflict resolution, log search, clone, fetch, push and pull, remotes, worktrees, submodules, external diff and merge tools, identity profiles, commit signing, and pull requests on GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud. Everything is on the feature reference , and every screen is on the screen reference . And then it runs the agents The agent farm takes a goal, cuts it into tasks, and hands them to the coding agents already on your PATH — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Oh My Pi, or anything else with a command line. Each task gets its own branch and its own worktree. Verification runs your repository's commands. Review is performed by a different agent than the one that wrote the change. Neither can be skipped by an agent's own report. The rule the farm is built around An agent saying “done” is not done. There is no transition from an agent's own report straight to Done : verification and a peer review are in the path, and nothing in the codebase can route around them. Nothing leaves the machine unless you ask There is no telemetry, no analytics, no account of ours and no server of ours in the path. Nothing in Spagitty is a model and nothing here ships a key. Repositories stay on disk; forge tokens live in the OS keychain. The whole of it is written up under privacy & security , along with the two boundaries — one process spawner, one HTTP client — that make those claims checkable rather than promised. Reading the source The repository is meant to be read, not only run. If you are here for the code, these four pages are the map: Code map Every directory and module in the workspace, and where to start reading. spagitty-core Every git operation, module by module — and the gix / git boundary. spagitty-farm The farm's control plane: model, adapters, workspaces, orchestration, verification, review. The frontend One store per screen, one module that calls invoke , and a shared UI kit. How we work Alongside the product code we keep a working record: why a change existed, what was verified, and what broke along the way. It lives in the repository under agile/ rather than in someone's head, and a test fails if the index and the tree disagree. The how we work page describes it; CI/CD & releases describes the six gates every change clears; testing says what is checked and what is deliberately not. Status 0.x. The surface is not yet stable — a MINOR bump may break it. Every screen in the design handoff is built, the farm is built on top of them, and the release lane tags from the changelog. What remains open is named on the screen that defers it rather than left out. Where to go next FAQ What it costs, what it sends, which agents it runs, how it compares. Glossary Spagitty's own vocabulary, and the git terms it leans on. Contributing What to read first, how a branch is named, and what a pull request needs. h.t: It reads, reviews and lands the work
An agent's own report is not evidence
Say what a thing does, including when it does nothing
Git is the authority, not our preferences
The destructive thing is the one that asks

b: Start here What Spagitty is A local-first desktop Git client for repositories where people and coding agents commit side by side, and the gateway to a Git-managed agent farm. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, it is free software under the GPL, and it has no account, no server and no model of its own. The problem Work arrives faster than it can be read. A repository where several people and several coding agents are all committing produces history at a rate that outstrips anybody's ability to follow it in a terminal, and the tools most of us reach for were designed for a slower shape of work — one author, one branch at a time, a review that happens once at the end. What breaks first is not the writing. It is the reading : what happened, who did it, whether it was checked, and what to do next. A repository without a readable history is a plate of tangled pasta. Spagitty straightens the strands. Where the name comes from Spagitty — spa-gi-ty — is spaghetti plus Git. It is also the mark: four dark strands that begin tangled at the top of an amber plate and resolve into straight, parallel paths below. The metaphor is kept literal on purpose. Tangled and straightened, pasta and strands. We do not extend it into chefs and kitchens in product copy; that register belongs to the delight layer , where it is deliberately a joke. What it does Two things, and the second is built on the first. It reads, reviews and lands the work Spagitty is a full desktop Git client: a lane graph of history with hide, solo, pin and smart visibility; a working copy that stages by file, hunk or line; diffs with syntax highlighting, image comparison and binary size deltas; file history with rename following and a blame gutter; branches, tags, stashes, the reflog, worktrees and submodules as first-class screens; interactive rebase with a preview before anything runs; in-app conflict resolution or your own merge tool; and pull requests read, reviewed, created and merged against GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud. See the feature reference for the whole list. It runs the agents Set a goal. Spagitty cuts it into tasks and hands them to the coding agents already installed on your machine, up to eight at a time, each on its own branch in its own worktree. Verification runs your repository's own commands in the task's worktree. Review is performed by a different agent than the one that wrote the change. You choose where you stand, from Manual — nothing runs by itself — to Unattended . The whole feature is written up on the agent farm . The principles Local-first, and checkably so Repositories stay on disk. There is no account step, no cloud to log into, and no server of ours in any path. The only network boundary in the whole workspace is one file — crates/spagitty-core/src/forge/http.rs — talking to the forges you connected, when you ask it to. A test asserts that exactly one HTTP client exists, that it is declared only in that crate, and that the webview links none at all. Nothing here is a model Spagitty ships no model and no API key. The agents it runs are programs already on your machine, invoked as you, with your credentials. We never describe Spagitty as “AI-powered”, because that trades away the one thing a local-first tool has: you can tell what it is doing. An agent's own report is not evidence The farm's status machine has no edge from “the agent said it finished” to Done . Verification runs the repository's own commands; review is performed by a second agent; and every handoff goes through Spagitty rather than between agents, so there is one audit trail and one place that decides what happens next. Say what a thing does, including when it does nothing A toggle that is not honoured yet names the item that will honour it. A screen that cannot do something says so where you would look for it, rather than failing silently when clicked. “May conflict” on the rebase preview uses the word may , because knowing for certain would mean performing the merges — and claiming a clean result we cannot prove would be the worse lie. Git is the authority, not our preferences Whether a commit will be signed is read from commit.gpgsign and its neighbours, not from a Spagitty setting pretending to be that. Branch names are validated by git, because a second implementation of check-ref-format could only disagree with it. Clearing an identity field runs git config --unset rather than writing an empty string, because a configured empty email is a different thing from an unset one. The destructive thing is the one that asks Staging, unstaging and committing only move work forward, so they do not interrupt. Discard, delete, reset --hard , force push and rebase do, and the confirmation says what actually goes away — including, where it applies, the exact command that brings it back. What Spagitty is not Not this Why A hosted forge GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket stay outside. Spagitty reads and writes to them through a token you issue. A CI system Verification runs your repository's commands locally, in a task's worktree. It is a gate, not a pipeline. A model, or a wrapper around one No inference happens in Spagitty. The agents are separate programs you installed. A productivity leaderboard The badge screen ranks agents by first-pass rate in this repository, never by volume, and never puts a human on the same table. A telemetry surface Nothing is counted, sampled or sent. There is nowhere for it to go. Who it is for People who review more than they write. The graph is the primary navigation surface rather than a read-only report — almost every operation is one right-click away from a commit or a branch label. People supervising coding agents. The farm is a supervision screen: a plan on the left, the selected task in the middle, and what just happened along the bottom, so supervising does not mean navigating. People learning how a desktop Git application is put together. The architecture is three layers with hard seams, and the working record

d: Download a build for Linux, macOS or Windows, open your first repository, or build Spagitty from source with Rust and Bun.

h.t: Opening a repository straight from the command line
If the window comes up blank on Linux

b: Start here Install & first run Spagitty ships installers for Linux, macOS and Windows on every publishing merge. There is no account step and no cloud to log into — install it, open a repository, and work. Download a build Every release carries installers for all three platforms, built by the release lane rather than by hand: Latest release All releases Platform What you get Notes Linux .deb , .rpm and .AppImage Needs the platform WebView, WebKitGTK. Most desktop distributions already have it. macOS .dmg and .app Apple silicon on the published release. The draft lane also builds an Intel binary. Windows .msi and .exe installer Uses the system WebView2 runtime. Nothing is signed yet There is no Apple Developer account and no code-signing certificate in this project, so macOS Gatekeeper refuses a downloaded build on a double-click and Windows SmartScreen warns about it. On macOS, open it once from the context menu — right-click the app, choose Open , then Open again in the dialog. On Windows, choose More info → Run anyway . Adding real signing is a change to the build gate and the draft lane together, and it is tracked rather than quietly deferred. First run Open a repository. The tab strip's + , the toolbar's repository picker, or the All repositories screen all do it. Spagitty never goes looking for repositories on its own — opening one is the only way it joins the list. The graph paints as it walks. Rows arrive in batches from a worker thread and never move once drawn, so a large repository is readable long before the walk finishes. Set your identity, if you want to. Settings → You reads user.name and user.email per scope and says which file each value came from. Saved profiles let you switch between them from the status strip. Connect a forge, if you use one. Settings → You → Accounts takes a personal access token for GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket Cloud. The token goes into the OS keychain and never into a configuration file. Pick a theme. Settings → Appearance has eight palette families, each in light and dark. See themes & appearance . Two things worth learning early Ctrl/Cmd+P opens the command palette — everything Spagitty can do, filtered as you type. Ctrl+F goes straight to log search from any screen, with the first field focused. Where Spagitty keeps things What Where Recent repositories A plain JSON file of paths in Spagitty's own configuration directory Behaviour toggles Beside the repository list, in the same directory Connected accounts accounts.json — a host and a login, and nothing else Forge tokens The OS keychain. Never a configuration file. Theme, column layouts, badge records localStorage in the webview, keyed by repository path An agent farm .spagitty/ inside the repository, excluded from git and never committed Build from source You need Rust 1.77 or newer , Bun 1.4 , and the platform WebView. git clone https://github.com/spa-git-ty/spagitty.git cd spagitty bun install bun run check # typecheck: svelte-kit sync && svelte-check bun run test # vitest bun run coverage # vitest with the coverage floor enforced cargo test --workspace # the Rust suites bun run tauri dev # the desktop app, in development bun run tauri build # installers for this platform On Linux you also need the WebKitGTK development packages that Tauri links against. The Tauri prerequisites list them per distribution; nothing in Spagitty adds to that list. Opening a repository straight from the command line The binary takes a path and opens onto it with no dialog. In development the argument has to be passed through both wrappers: bun run tauri dev -- -- -- /path/to/repository That path is read by the launch_path command, which is also what the session restore falls back to when no path is given — see the launch sequence . If the window comes up blank on Linux WebKitGTK's DMABuf renderer cannot allocate a GBM buffer on some driver and compositor combinations, and a webview with no frame to present is a white window for the whole session. The symptom is a blank window with Failed to create GBM buffer on stderr. The workaround is one environment variable, and it is opt-in rather than forced on every Linux host: WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 spagitty Spagitty sets WEBKIT_FORCE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1 for itself unless your environment already has an opinion, and deliberately sets nothing for the DMABuf renderer — turning it off for everybody costs every host the GPU path, which is a frame that lags the pointer during a resize. The reasoning is in the Tauri layer . Running the gates locally Gates 1 to 3 are what a change is checked against before it is committed. The full list, and what each one proves, is on CI/CD & releases . bun install --frozen-lockfile # the dependencies, locked cargo deny check licenses bans sources # gate 1 — needs cargo-deny cargo fmt --all --check # gate 2 cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings bun run check python3 tools/make-icons.py --check # gate 2 — brand drift, needs Pillow python3 tools/make-brand.py --check cargo llvm-cov --workspace \ --ignore-filename-regex '(fixture|testing)\.rs' --summary-only bun run coverage # gate 3 cargo deny check advisories # gate 4 bun audit --audit-level=high cargo-deny and cargo-llvm-cov install with: cargo install cargo-deny cargo-llvm-cov Updating Settings → About checks whether there is a newer Spagitty than the one you are running. It is a check, not an updater: it tells you a version exists and where to get it, and nothing downloads or replaces anything behind your back.

d: Every capability Spagitty ships, grouped by what you are trying to do: the graph, the working copy, diffs, branches, rebasing, pull requests, the farm and the chrome.
b: Start here Feature reference Everything Spagitty ships, grouped by what you are trying to do. Each group links to the screen it lives on and, where the reasoning is interesting, to the page that explains it. Reading history The commit graph Streamed and virtualised. Rows arrive in batches from a worker thread and never move once drawn, so a repository with a hundred thousand commits is readable immediately. The lane column is drawn on a canvas covering only the visible window — a repository with 200,000 commits draws the same number of paths as one with 40. Lanes, branches and tags. Branch and tag chips sit in a gutter of their own, starting at the column's left edge so every row's first chip is at the same x. A branch chip carries its own divergence. Author portraits, generated locally. A node is a portrait computed from the author's email — never fetched. A picture per author would be a request per author on the most performance-sensitive screen, would hand the committer list to whoever was asked, and would make an offline repository look different from an online one. A merge is a plain dot rather than a face: it is where two lines join, not one person's work. Noise control. Hide, solo, smart branch visibility and pin-to-left, all per repository. Each resolves to a root set for a fresh walk rather than a filter over drawn rows, so lanes never draw an edge between commits that are not parent and child. The header chip always names the current scope and the gear lists what is hidden, with a way back. A configurable table. Branch/Tag, Graph, Commit Message, Author, Date/Time and SHA. Right-click the header to toggle, drag to reorder, drag a divider to resize — choice, order and widths saved per repository. Depth that stays readable. Past twelve lanes the pitch compresses rather than the column widening, down to a floor, so the graph can never reach the message column. Node radius follows the pitch down. Log search Author, message, path, date range and diff content, composing as AND, each rendered as a chip that says exactly what is applied. Results stream as the walk finds them, and every query carries a token so starting one cancels the one before — which is what makes it safe to search on a keystroke. The path filter uses git's own simplification rule, so a merge is not listed for a change it only carried across. File history and blame A file's commit timeline with rename following ( --follow ), beside a line-by-line blame gutter carrying author, commit and relative time. Hovering a commit in the timeline highlights every line it introduced; commit chips link back into the graph. The reflog Where a ref has been — HEAD or any local branch — with three ways out of an entry: branch here, check out here, reset here, offered in that order because only the first cannot cost anything. Changing the working copy Stage and unstage by file, hunk or line. Staged sits above Unstaged as solid rows over dashed ones, and a path appears in both when it is staged in part. Discard, with a clear account of what goes away. File, hunk or everything, only on the unstaged side, each behind a confirmation whose wording says whether the file is reverted or deleted. The staged side is deliberately untouched: unstage first, which costs nothing. Commit, with signing read from git. The Commit button counts staged changes, not working ones — a working copy with ten changed files and one staged must not offer to commit ten. Diffs Unified and split views of the same data, with the choice shared across the screens that show diffs, because it is a preference about reading diffs rather than about a screen. Syntax highlighting across a dozen grammars, mapped onto the active theme's own palette tokens rather than a fixed colour set. Image comparison — side by side, swipe, and onion skin. Binary files report a size delta rather than pretending to have lines. Search inside the patch text , so a large diff can be navigated rather than scrolled. Your own tools. External diff and merge tools are discovered on PATH and configured through git's own diff.tool and merge.tool keys — VS Code, Meld, Beyond Compare, KDiff3, Sublime Merge, Vimdiff and others. Branches of work Thing What you can do Branches A sortable, resizable table with two-sided divergence bars; create, rename, delete, bulk-clean merged branches; checkout through git switch . Merged branches render dashed — except the one you are on. Tags A screen of their own: create, delete, rewrite an annotated message, check out. Annotated and lightweight are told apart throughout, because the difference decides whether a message can exist. Stashes List, pop, apply, drop, and browse an entry file by file with its diff — a stash is a commit, so the Diff screen's own components render it. Worktrees List, add (new branch, existing branch or detached), lock and unlock with a reason, remove and prune. Reachable from the tab strip and the command palette. Submodules Status, recursive init and update, URL sync, and deinit. Remotes Add, rename, remove and retarget, each through git remote rather than a config edit. Rewriting and repairing Interactive rebase Plan a history rewrite and see the result before anything runs. The todo list is generated , not parsed — running git rebase -i to read the file it opens would start the rebase this screen exists to avoid. The preview is a fold of the plan, recomputed after every edit, so the plan and the picture of it cannot disagree. Rows move by drag and from the keyboard. “May conflict” is marked as a heuristic, in that word. Conflict resolution Ours, the merged result and theirs side by side, with the common ancestor behind a disclosure — all four read from the index's stages, which is the whole data model. Which stages exist is the kind of conflict, and a missing side says so rather than rendering an empty pane. Three ways out of a file: take a whole side, take one marker region, or type into the merged pane, each followed by an explicit git add

d: A goal, the tasks it was cut into, and the coding agents on your machine working them in parallel — one branch and one worktree each, verified and peer-reviewed before anything merges.

h.t: Tasks that turn out to be too big
A branch and a worktree per task
A queued task says why it is not running
A quiet run says so, and is never stopped for you

b: Using Spagitty The agent farm Set a goal. Cut it into tasks. Watch several agents work them at once, on branches you can read in the graph you already trust. The farm is Spagitty's own subject — everything else in the application is where its output is read. Three rules the whole feature is built around An agent saying “done” is not done. There is no transition from an agent's own report to Done : verification and a review by a different agent are in the path and cannot be skipped. Agents never talk to each other. Every handoff goes through Spagitty, so there is one audit trail and one place that decides what happens next. Nothing an agent does reaches your checkout. Every task runs in its own worktree on its own branch. Agents, not models Spagitty runs agents; it does not contain them. There is no model here and no key. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Oh My Pi are detected on your PATH , and anything else with a command line can be added by hand. They run as you, with your credentials, on your machine. Provider How it is invoked Why that form Claude Code claude -p <prompt> Print mode runs the whole turn to completion with no terminal attached and writes the transcript to standard output. Codex codex exec <prompt> exec is the non-interactive subcommand: it runs the turn and exits. Bare codex would open a session. Cursor cursor-agent Not cursor — that is the editor, and running it here would open a window instead of doing the work. Oh My Pi Prompt on standard input Its command line does not take a prompt argument in the shape the others do. Anything else A command you configure A custom adapter, so a new provider is a settings change rather than a release. Detection walks PATH itself rather than shelling out to which , and the registry keeps two things apart on purpose: what this machine has , and what you have said about it — the role you want an agent to play, whether it is enabled, and any argument overrides. The loop A goal. One sentence, plus any constraints you want honoured. It lives longer than a single run. A plan. An agent turns the goal into tasks. They arrive as drafts , so a person reads a decomposition before several agents act on it. A band above the list says how many were proposed, with a checkbox each: add them all, add the ones you want, or discard. Assignment. The router maps a task's kind to a preferred role, the registry finds an agent for that role, and if nobody holds it the task goes to whoever can code. Work. The task gets a branch and a worktree of its own; the agent runs there, and what it says is narrated into lines a person can watch. Verification. Your repository's own commands, run in that worktree, stopping at the first failure. Review. A second agent — never the one that wrote the change — reads it and returns a decision. Merge. Depending on where you have put the autonomy dial, either you merge it or the farm does. Where you stand Five autonomy levels. The setting is a sentence about where you are, not a slider labelled “risk”. Level What happens Manual Spagitty organises the tasks. Nothing runs by itself. Assisted Agents run; you approve every task. This is the default. Semi-automatic Agents run and review each other; you approve the merges. Automatic Verified low-risk tasks may merge themselves. Unattended Everything, without you. Even at the top of the dial An automatic merge still requires passing checks, a successful independent review of the work actually committed, and merge permission. Competing farm merges serialise rather than racing, and a task keeps its intended destination. A task A task is machine-readable on purpose: the farm never relies entirely on free-form prose. It carries a kind, its dependencies, the files it expects to touch, its own verification commands, and the record of every run against it. Kinds Architecture , Backend , Frontend , Testing , Documentation , Research , Review , Integration , General . The kind is what routes the task to a role — architect, backend, frontend, tester, reviewer, researcher, or general. Statuses Status Means Draft Written, but not yet part of the plan the farm will execute. Ready In the plan. Dependencies unsatisfied, or no agent free. Assigned An agent has it; the run has not started. Running An agent is working. Waiting Finished its run and is waiting on something outside itself — a dependency, a lease, a person. Blocked Cannot proceed and needs a person or a new task. Distinct from Failed : nothing went wrong, something is missing. Review With a second agent. Verification Running the repository's checks. Done Verified, reviewed and finished. Failed Something went wrong. Retryable, up to the farm's attempt limit. Cancelled Stopped on purpose. Who asked for it A farm mixes work you decided on with work a model produced, and after twenty tasks they look identical. Your own tasks stay unmarked; anything an agent asked for carries one quiet mark, and its panel says which agent and why — cut out of the goal, cut out of another task, or proposed while working on something else and asked for by nobody. Tasks that turn out to be too big Break it down asks an agent to cut one task into smaller ones. They arrive as a proposed plan under it, and the task becomes a heading that finishes when they do. Deleting the heading keeps the work that was under it. A branch and a worktree per task Named spagitty-farm/<task>/<provider> — for example spagitty-farm/TASK-0042/claude . The name is derived , never chosen, and derived in exactly one place, because it is how the commit graph, the worktree list and the Farm screen find each other. A glob over that prefix cleans up a whole farm without touching anything you named yourself. Two agents in two worktrees cannot corrupt each other's files — that is what the worktrees are for. What they can do is both edit the same path and produce two changes that conflict on the way back, so the workspace layer holds path-level leases : a task declares the files it expects to touch,

d: Every screen in Spagitty by its code — Graph, Diff, Working copy, Conflicts, Rebase, Branches, Stash, Pull requests, Log, Repositories, Settings, Clone, Reflog, Tags, History, Badges, Farm.
b: Using Spagitty Screen reference Every screen carries a short code — 1A , 1B , … — so it can be named in one token in a commit message or a conversation. The codes and their order come from the design handoff and are declared in src/lib/nav.ts . Code Screen Route In the rail 1A Graph / yes 1B Diff /diff no 1C Working copy /changes yes 1D Conflicts /conflicts yes 1E Interactive rebase /rebase yes 1F Branches /branches yes 1G Stash /stash yes 1H Pull requests /requests yes 1I Log search /search yes 1J All repositories /repos yes 1K Settings /settings yes 1L Clone modal no 1M Reflog /reflog yes 1N Tags /tags yes 1O File history /history no 1P Badges /badges yes 1Q Farm /farm yes 1A–1L is the whole of the design handoff, and all of it is built. 1M and 1N were not in the handoff at all — the Reflog and Tags came out of a gap analysis rather than the design, so they are numbered after the handoff's run rather than inserted into it, and a code still says where a screen came from. 1P came from neither: every other screen answers a question about the state of a repository, and Badges answers what has been done in one, and by whom. 1Q is the first screen about work that has not happened yet. The chrome Persistent across every screen. Title bar — repository name, current branch, build identity, window buttons. The window is undecorated, so the title bar is also the drag handle, and the application draws its own resize edges. It carries no theme control: Settings → Appearance is the one place the theme is set, and one preference with two controls is two things to keep in step. Toolbar — repository and branch pickers, Undo/Redo, Clone, Fetch, Push, Branch, Stash, Rebase, and the primary Commit button. Anything not built yet says so on hover rather than failing silently when clicked. Nav rail — the only answer to “where am I”: the active item and the route are the same fact. Counts are right-aligned, and · means “not computed yet”. The Farm takes the top slot — it is the product's own subject, and everything below it is where the farm's output is read. Status strip — one line along the bottom, in two groups with a rule between: what is changing (the walk, the working copy, the last fetch) and what is merely true (commits, tags, submodules). Reading them as one dot-separated run made “1 changed file” look like the same kind of fact as “Tags 42”. Key names are written in their Ctrl / Alt form throughout. The one exception is the command palette, which picks its notation from the platform at runtime — macOS is a build target, and printing Ctrl+ on a machine with no such key would be wrong in the other direction. 1A Graph route / src/routes/+page.svelte src/lib/graph/ The centre of gravity, and the application's primary navigation surface rather than a read-only report: almost every operation Spagitty can perform is reachable from a right-click here. A streamed, virtualised commit list with a lane canvas, a configurable column table and a detail panel. Rows arrive in batches from a worker thread and never move once drawn. Clicking selects; double-clicking opens the diff. Operations Right-click a commit for create-branch/tag-here, reset (soft/mixed/hard, named by effect rather than by flag), revert, cherry-pick, rebase-onto, detached checkout and copy-SHA. Right-click a branch label for merge, rebase, fast-forward, rename, delete, pin, hide and solo. Dragging one label onto another offers the three integration verbs, with the gesture carrying the direction. Shift and Ctrl/Cmd build a second selection — separate from the detail panel's — that cherry-picks a group or rebases a range. Nodes and lanes A node is the author's portrait, generated from their email and never fetched: the face is a function of the address, so it is the same on every machine and every launch. One description, two renderers — canvas for the node, CSS gradients for the Author column — so a person has one face on screen. A merge is a plain dot; putting the merge author's portrait on it would claim they wrote the branch it swallowed. The lane column is a surface of its own, bounded by a hairline, painted twice from one declaration: by each row, so it scrolls with them, and by a bed laid out once at the full height of the table underneath. The bed is what a repository shorter than the window needs. d: No telemetry, no account, no server of ours. Where tokens live, what crosses the network, and the two boundaries that make those claims checkable.

h.t: What does cross the network, and when
Two boundaries that make it checkable
One HTTP client, in one file

Why a personal access token rather than OAuth

b: Using Spagitty Privacy & security Spagitty has no telemetry, no analytics, no account of ours and no server of ours in any path. Repositories stay on disk. This page says exactly what that means, and — more usefully — how the claims are made checkable rather than promised. What Spagitty does not do No telemetry. Nothing is counted, sampled, batched or sent. There is nowhere for it to go. No analytics, crash reporting or usage metrics. Same reason. No account. There is no Spagitty sign-in, because there is no Spagitty service. No model, no key. Nothing in Spagitty performs inference, and nothing ships a credential for a provider. No repository upload. Repositories are read where they sit. Nothing copies, syncs or indexes them anywhere. No password prompt of our own. Credentials go through git's own helpers, which is where OS keychain integration already lives. What does cross the network, and when What To where When Pull request data The forge you connected — GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket Cloud When the Pull requests screen refreshes, carrying a token you issued, asking for pull requests you can already see in a browser. No repository contents, no paths, no commit messages. Fetch, push, pull, clone The remote in your repository's own config When you press the button. It is git doing it, with your credentials. An update check The releases API for this project When you ask, from Settings → About. It reports that a version exists; nothing downloads or replaces anything. Whatever an agent does Wherever that agent talks to Only in a farm run you started, and only for the agents you installed. Spagitty is not in that path — it starts a process, reads its output, and stops it. That is the complete list. Two boundaries that make it checkable A promise about what an application sends is only as good as the number of places that could send something. Spagitty keeps both counts at one. One HTTP client, in one file The original promise was that no HTTP client was linked in either language, with a test to keep it that way. Reading pull requests could not survive that, so it became a narrower promise that is still worth having and is still tested: exactly one client, ureq , declared only in spagitty-core , and reachable from exactly one file — crates/spagitty-core/src/forge/http.rs . The webview links no HTTP client, makes no request, and never holds a token. Its content security policy allows self , data URIs and Tauri's own asset protocol, and nothing else — so even a rendered pull request description cannot reach out. One process spawner, in one file crates/spagitty-core/src/shell.rs is the only module in the workspace that spawns a process. That is a correctness rule first — see the git binary boundary — but it is also what makes “what did this application actually run” answerable at all. Where secrets live Secret Stored Forge personal access tokens The OS keychain, and nowhere else. Never a configuration file. Remote credentials Not by Spagitty at all — git's credential helpers own them. Connected accounts accounts.json holds a host and a login. Nothing else. Why a personal access token rather than OAuth A token is issued, scoped and revoked by you without touching anything else you own. OAuth would need a redirect listener and a client secret shipped inside a GPL binary anybody can read — which is not a secret. The login is read back from the host rather than typed, so the account shown is the account the token actually belongs to. Credentials are removed on the way in A clone URL can carry a token — https://user:token@host/repo.git — so the command record strips the userinfo before the entry is stored. An entry that never held the secret cannot leak it through the copy button, or through a later reader who assumed display was doing the work. The agent farm Agents run as you. Same user, same environment, same credentials. Spagitty adds no key and no model. Each task is isolated to its own worktree. Nothing an agent does reaches your working copy, and path-level leases stop two agents editing the same file. The farm's state stays in the repository — .spagitty/ , added to .git/info/exclude , never committed, deleted with the repository. Verification runs argv, not a shell string. There is no shell in the verification path, so a command cannot be turned into three by a stray character. Stopping means stopping. Cancelling a run or reaching a deadline terminates the whole process tree — a process group on Unix, a job object on Windows, assigned before the child can spawn anything of its own. What Spagitty cannot promise for you A coding agent you run is a program with your permissions, talking to whatever service it was built for. Spagitty isolates its working tree and records what it did; it does not, and cannot, sandbox what that agent sends to its own provider. Choose the agents you install, and use the autonomy dial that matches how much you trust them. Supply chain Every dependency's licence is identified and permitted, checked on every change. Known-vulnerable dependencies fail the build at the high level or above, and an advisory that cannot be fixed is recorded by id , with its crate and its reason, so anything not listed still fails — the line between recording a risk and switching the check off. Secret scanning runs over every change. The whole contract is on CI/CD & releases . Reporting something Spagitty is free software and the source is the specification: if you believe something here is wrong, the file that would prove it is named on this page. Open an issue on the repository . For a suspected vulnerability, say what the class of problem is rather than posting a working exploit.

b: How it is built Architecture Three layers, and each knows nothing about the one above it. That is why the git core can be tested without a window, and why a screen that looks broken is almost always a store bug rather than a Rust one. No window handles, no events, no app state — so it compiles and is tested without a GUI. Only shell.rs spawns a process. One place knows what was executed. Only forge/http.rs makes a network request. One place knows what was sent. Crossing the boundary Types that cross to the frontend derive Serialize with #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] , and are mirrored by hand in src/lib/types.ts . The two are kept in step deliberately rather than generated, because the wire shape is small and a generator would be more machinery than the problem needs. Errors cross as plain strings. Error 's Display text is therefore user-facing — plain, specific, no stack-trace jargon — and screens show that string directly rather than substituting a message of their own. Every command and every event is catalogued on the IPC reference . The git binary boundary The rule, in one sentence: If the operation mutates state that the wider git ecosystem also reads, or delegates to something outside the repository, it shells out to git . The one function that does not wait shell::clone_start is the only spawn that does not wait for git to finish: a clone runs for minutes, reports progress as it goes, and has to be cancellable, so the caller owns the child process. Everything else in the module is a command that ends. That location is the whole point of the feature. A screen composing its own “the command behind this button” string would be describing what it asked for : it would not know that a fetch carries --prune --progress , that a force push is --force-with-lease , or that reverting a merge gained -m 1 on the way down. The record is written where the process is started, so it is evidence rather than a claim, and every spawn goes through the same two functions so a new one cannot quietly skip it. Reads are absent, deliberately. Log walking, refs, diff and status are in-process and have no command line. Nothing is synthesised for them, and the panel says so. d: The Rust crate that performs every git operation — module by module, including the gix/git binary boundary and the forge network boundary.

h.t: The one read that breaks the rule

b: How it is built spagitty-core Every git operation Spagitty performs. UI-agnostic: no Tauri, no window handles, no events — so the crate compiles and is tested without a GUI, and its examples run it from a terminal. cargo run -p spagitty-core --example graph-dump -- /path/to/repo cargo run -p spagitty-core --example diff-dump -- /path/to/repo The git binary boundary shell.rs is the only module in the workspace that spawns a process. The rule: If the operation mutates state that the wider git ecosystem also reads, or delegates to something outside the repository, it shells out to git . Read-only history questions are answered in-process with gix . So reads — log walking, refs, diffing, status, the index's conflict stages — are gix . Interactive rebase execution, hooks, LFS, submodule recursion, credential helpers, committing, staging, checkout, stash push, writing git config and cloning are git . The table in that module's header is the authority, and it is extended in the same change that adds an operation to it. gix is MIT/Apache-2.0, which links cleanly into a GPL-3 program. The one read that breaks the rule shell::blame shells out, and it is written down rather than quietly done. gix::blame 0.16 — the newest published version — panics on an ordinary history shape: a file blamed at a merge commit whose history contains an intervening commit that left the file alone. Every diff algorithm and both rename settings do it. The exception carries an end condition: blame moves back in-process when the upstream defect is fixed. It is the only read in the workspace that spawns a process. The one spawn that does not wait shell::clone_start . A clone runs for minutes, reports progress as it goes, and has to be cancellable, so the caller owns the child process. Everything else in the module is a command that ends. Reading a repository repo.rs Opening a repository and describing it. open , open_sync , summary , workdir , info , last_fetched , head . RepoSummary is what the All repositories screen reads for a card without opening the repository as the current one. graph.rs History walking and lane assignment. walk , walk_pinned , all_tips , tips_for . Carries ROW_PITCH — the constant duplicated across the language boundary on purpose, with a test that reads the TypeScript file and fails with both values named if they drift — plus LaneEdge , GraphRow , RowLanes and the batch size the worker emits in. refs.rs RefIndex — commit id to the refs pointing at it, built once per refresh and handed to the walk, so attaching chips to a row is a hash lookup rather than a ref scan per commit. status.rs The working-copy status walk and the counts the nav rail shows. Only the counts whose screens exist are computed for real; the rest are None , and the rail renders · rather than a number that would be wrong. search.rs Finding commits. The same revision walk the graph does, with a predicate and without lanes — not a second traversal of history. Query , SearchRow , walk . blame.rs Who last touched each line, parsed from git blame --line-porcelain , plus the file history walk behind screen 1O. What this module owns is the part git does not do: deciding what is worth blaming at all. NotBlamable distinguishes a binary file, a missing path and a directory — an empty list would read as a file nobody has ever touched. Diffs diff.rs Three levels, because they cost different amounts: commit_detail (the message and the people), commit_diff (the file list and its totals), file_diff (one file's hunks). Also the working-copy variants, the hunk patch a stage-hunk needs, and binary_file_diff / binary_working_diff , which report a size delta and a MIME type rather than pretending a binary has lines. Writing work.rs Changing the working copy: stage , unstage , stage_hunk , unstage_hunk , discard , discard_hunk , commit . Reading the working copy lives in status.rs ; this is the writing half, and every operation goes through shell . ops.rs Every history operation the graph offers: reset , revert , cherry_pick , integrate (merge / rebase / fast-forward, as one Integration enum), rebase_onto , the interactive-rebase lifecycle, checkout_detached , branch rename and delete, tag create and delete, the stash actions, fetch , pull and push . Each is a thin, named wrapper over shell — the naming is the point, because reset(Hard) reads at the call site and --hard does not. shell.rs The boundary itself. Around sixty functions, each one a git invocation, each one recorded as it finishes. ResetMode and PullMode live here because they are the shapes of git's own flags. Branches, tags, stashes, the reflog branches.rs BranchRow , list , divergences , checkout , create . Ahead and behind are counted against the remote-tracking ref on disk, which is whatever the last fetch left there: nothing here talks to a network, so the numbers are exact for what is known locally and cannot be more current than that — and the screen says so rather than implying it is live. The list re-opens the repository rather than reusing the session handle, because gix reads config once at open time and a branch's upstream lives in config. tags.rs tags , create , delete , retag . Annotated and lightweight are told apart throughout, because that difference decides whether a message can exist at all. stash.rs A stash is not a special kind of object: it is a commit whose first parent is the commit the work was made on, and refs/stash is an ordinary ref whose reflog is the list. push refuses the nothing-to-save case with a reason, because succeeding quietly reads from a button as a stash that happened and then vanished. reflog.rs Where a ref has been. logged_refs , reflog , and the three ways back to a point in it. worktrees.rs List, add, remove, lock, unlock, prune — parsing git's --porcelain stream, with the parser exposed so it can be tested against captured output rather than a live repository. submodules.rs Status, recursive init and update, URL sync, deinit — same shape, sam

d: The agent farm's control plane: the model, adapters, workspaces, execution, orchestration, verification, review and persistence.
b: How it is built spagitty-farm The agent farm's control plane: a goal, the tasks it was cut into, and the agents working them. It orchestrates and nothing else — every git operation it performs is spagitty-core 's, and it holds no Tauri types either. What the farm does , from the outside, is on the agent farm . This page is the crate. Three rules the crate is built around An agent saying “done” is not done. There is no transition from an agent's own report to Done ; verification and a review by a different agent are in the path and cannot be skipped. Agents never talk to each other. Every handoff goes through the service, so there is one audit trail and one place that decides what happens next. Nothing an agent does reaches the user's checkout. Every task runs in its own worktree on its own branch. model/ — the vocabulary Everything here is data. No process is spawned, no file is written and no git command runs from this module tree — deliberately, because these types are what everything else agrees on. model/farm.rs Farm , FarmStatus , Autonomy (Manual, Assisted, Semi-automatic, Automatic, Unattended) and Permissions . A farm belongs to a repository, and there is one open at a time. model/goal.rs One sentence from the user plus the constraints they want honoured. Separate from Farm because a goal outlives a run. model/task.rs Task , TaskStatus (11 states), TaskKind (9 kinds), TaskPriority and TaskOrigin — the last being what lets the screen show who asked for a task. A task is machine-readable on purpose: “never rely entirely on free-form prose” is what makes the difference between a farm and a chat window. model/agent.rs AgentDefinition , AgentProvider , AgentCapability , AgentRole , AgentInputMode , AgentAvailability . An agent must not be represented only by the path to its executable — the reason shows up the first time two of them are the same binary with different arguments. model/run.rs One execution of one agent against one task. A task can be run more than once — a review asking for changes, a verification failure, a retry after a crash — so the run is the record, not the task. model/handoff.rs What an agent hands back, in a fenced structure every agent returns: status, a test report, proposed tasks. Both halves matter — the structure, so Spagitty can act, and the prose, so a person can read what happened. model/event.rs FarmEvent — one internally-tagged enum rather than a Tauri event per kind, because the screen keeps one activity list and one ordering. Sixteen variants, from TaskCreated through VerificationFinished and ReviewCompleted to MergeCompleted . Recorded wraps one with the time it happened, which is what makes a log a log. agent/ — the providers Nothing above this module knows the name of a provider's executable or the shape of its command line. Each adapter knows exactly one thing: how to invoke its own CLI without a terminal. agent/adapter.rs The one interface every provider implements — AgentAdapter , AgentRunRequest , AgentCommand . Synchronous, with the reasoning in its header. adapters/claude.rs Claude Code, in print mode: claude -p <prompt> runs the whole turn to completion with no terminal attached and writes the transcript to standard output. adapters/codex.rs Codex. codex exec <prompt> is the non-interactive subcommand; bare codex would open a session. adapters/cursor.rs Cursor. The command is cursor-agent , not cursor — that is the editor, and running it here would open a window. adapters/pi.rs Oh My Pi, which takes its prompt on standard input. adapters/custom.rs An agent Spagitty has never heard of. A list of future providers is a list of releases if each one needs an adapter, so a configured command with a prompt token is a settings change instead. agent/detector.rs Finding what is installed. Walks PATH itself rather than shelling out — with the reasoning in its header. agent/registry.rs The join between two things that must not be confused: what this machine has , and what the user has said about it. workspace/ — where the work happens workspace/branch.rs Naming the branch and the directory a task works in — spagitty-farm/<task>/<provider> . Both names are derived, never chosen, and derived here , because the branch name is how the graph, the worktree list and the Farm screen find each other. task_of and provider_of read it back; a glob over NAMESPACE cleans up a farm without touching anything the user named. workspace/worktree.rs A working tree of its own for every task. Two agents in one checkout is not a race that shows up occasionally — it is one agent reading another's half-written file. FARM_DIR is .spagitty , added to .git/info/exclude so a farm is never committed. workspace/lock.rs Path-level leases. Worktrees stop two agents corrupting each other's files; leases stop two of them editing the same path and producing changes that conflict on the way back. EVERYTHING is the lease a task takes when it cannot say what it will touch. workspace/cleanup.rs Told what is left over rather than which task to clean — a different question from removing one worktree, and the one that matters after a crash. execution/ — running an agent execution/process.rs One thread per run rather than an async runtime, with the reasoning in its header. Cancellation , Session , Ended . execution/tree.rs A process tree owned by one run. Windows starts the child suspended so nothing can escape before job assignment; Unix assigns a process group at spawn. Stopping a run stops its descendants. execution/log.rs The transcript on disk rather than a String in memory — which is what lets the drawer read a task's whole log back after the fact, and what stops a long session growing. execution/narrate.rs Turning what an agent prints into something a person can watch. Verbatim for providers that emit plain text, ClaudeStream for a structured one. orchestrator/ — deciding what happens next The graph says what could run, the router says who would do it , and the scheduler puts the two toge

d: The thin shell that owns the window, the background workers and the command surface between the webview and the Rust crates.

h.t: Testing a layer that owns a window

b: How it is built The Tauri layer src-tauri owns the window, the command surface and the background workers. It is deliberately thin: it holds the open session — one repository at a time — and forwards to the core. No git logic lives here. The files lib.rs Command registration, and the run sequence. Owns the window and the workers; all git logic is spagitty-core 's. commands.rs One #[tauri::command] per operation. Holds the open session, forwards to the core, and converts errors to strings for the webview. farm.rs The farm's Tauri layer — thin in the same way. Holds the open farm, forwards to spagitty-farm , and turns each FarmEvent into one webview event. State of its own, with a different lifetime from the graph session. graph_worker.rs One thread per open repository, walking history and streaming rows. search_worker.rs One thread per query. Starting one cancels the one before. clone_worker.rs One thread per clone, owning the git process — so cancelling is a signal rather than a request. network_worker.rs Fetch and push, watched while they run. Both were fire-and-wait: --progress was passed to git and nothing read it. rebase_worker.rs One thread watching git rewrite history, so the session lock is never held while it runs. watch.rs Filesystem watching over the git directory. Spagitty does not poll — notify tells the UI when something it displays has actually changed. command_log.rs The adapter between record.rs and the window: one observer registered at startup, forwarding each entry as an event. recents.rs The repositories the user has opened. Application state, not repository state — a record of what the user did. settings.rs Spagitty's own preferences, beside the repository list. None of it is a fact about a repository. accounts.rs Which hosting accounts are connected — a host and a login. The token is in the keychain. profiles.rs Named identity profiles, and applying one locally or globally. about.rs Build identity and the dependency licence list — both halves of the GPL-3 obligation the About section exists to meet. platform.rs Host facts that must be true before the webview builds its first frame. Nothing here is git or Spagitty. testing.rs Scaffolding for this crate's own tests. Why the workers are threads Each long-running job owns a thread and its own cancellation, and each one is a slightly different shape for a reason its header explains: Worker What is different about it Graph One per open repository, long-lived. It walks lazily — the worker does nothing until the store asks for rows. Search One per query , not per repository. Starting one cancels the one before, and rows carrying a stale token are dropped rather than rendered — which is what makes searching on a keystroke safe. Clone Owns a child process rather than a walk, so cancellation is a signal. Removal of a partial clone happens after the child is reaped, never after the kill signal, or the two race and files reappear behind it. Network Exists so a fetch says something while it runs. It reads git's progress rather than waiting for the exit code. Rebase Runs without holding the session lock, with progress read from git's own state counters. Tokens, not cancellation races Both streaming workers stamp every batch with the token of the walk that produced it. A superseded walk is discarded by ignoring its rows rather than by successfully cancelling it in time — which is a race the frontend cannot win and does not have to. The farm's commands are async Its commands are #[tauri::command(async)] rather than plain, because they take locks that agent threads hold — and a blocking command runs on the thread that paints the window. A farm that planned for thirty seconds froze the window for thirty seconds. Platform facts platform.rs arranges the webview's environment as the first statement of run — before the builder, and while the process is still single-threaded, which is the only state in which setting an environment variable is sound. It sets WEBKIT_FORCE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1 , which keeps the whole page on the GPU rather than letting WebKitGTK fall back to software for the parts its heuristics misjudge. It deliberately does not set WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER , and that is a recorded reversal. It used to be set to 1 on every Linux start, because WebKitGTK's DMABuf renderer cannot allocate a GBM buffer on some driver and compositor combinations, and a webview with no frame to present is a white window for the whole session. The cost of that workaround was written down and then lived with for too long: with the renderer off, every Linux host repaints through shared memory, on the CPU — including the hosts that never had the bug. On a real window that is a frame that lags the pointer during a resize and a history that scrolls at a fraction of the display's rate. The accelerated path is the default now. A host that hits the GBM bug sets the variable in its own environment, which the process still honours — along with an explicit value for either variable in either direction. The command surface Around 130 commands, grouped by what they are for. The full list, with what each one does, is on the IPC reference . Group Shape The walk open_repo , close_repo , graph_request , graph_restart , graph_visibility , snapshot , metrics Reading Commit detail and diffs, the working copy, branches, stashes, blame, file history, conflicts, search Writing Stage, commit, checkout, branch and tag operations, reset, revert, cherry-pick, integrate, the rebase lifecycle, stash, fetch, push, pull Application state Recent repositories, clone planning and execution, about, licences, identity, profiles, settings, the launch path The forge Accounts, pull requests, files, commits, comments, reviews, merge, close, draft state The farm Around 35 commands, from farm_open through planning, tasks, running, verification, review and merge, to farm_sweep One special command graph_visibility is worth naming: hide, solo, smart visibility and pin-to-left all resolve

d: The SvelteKit app: one store per screen, the single API module, the shared UI kit, the metrics contract and the delight layer.

h.t: Three things are mounted once, by the shell

b: How it is built The frontend SvelteKit 2 in SPA mode — ssr = false , prerender = false . Tauri serves a static bundle from disk; there is no server. Svelte 5 runes throughout, TypeScript, built and tested with Bun. The rules Five, and they shape everything else src/lib/api.ts is the only module that calls invoke . A command rename is a one-file change. One directory per screen , each with a store.svelte.ts and its components. Stores export a single object with getters , never the $state variables themselves, so a screen cannot write another screen's state by accident. Structural numbers come from metrics.ts . There is no height: 26px in any component. Standard git terminology only. fetch, push, stage, hunk, stash@{n} , pick/squash/reword/drop, ours/theirs. No invented vocabulary, no friendly renaming of git concepts. Shared modules api.ts Typed wrappers around every Tauri command. Everything else talks in the types from types.ts . types.ts The wire types, mirroring the serde shapes in the Rust crates by hand. Kept in step deliberately rather than generated — the wire shape is small, and a generator would be more machinery than the problem needs. metrics.ts Structural numbers, the single source of truth, published as CSS custom properties by applyMetrics . Carries ROW_PITCH , which Rust reads back at boot and compares. nav.ts The rail: screen codes, order, labels, and which count each row shows. The active item and the route are the same fact. repo.svelte.ts The open repository — which one, what HEAD is, and the rail counts. One is open at a time; opening another replaces it, which on the Rust side tears down the previous walk and watcher. workspace.svelte.ts Repository tabs, including tabs onto linked worktrees. session.ts What a launch resumes, as a sequence a test can watch. themes.ts · theme.svelte.ts Sixteen palettes as data, and which one is applied. Switching writes custom properties — no component re-render, no stylesheet swap. scale.svelte.ts Text size (90–130%) and interface zoom (100–200%), two independent dials that compose. panels.svelte.ts The panel registry: each panel names its CSS variable, its anchored edge and its range. Splitter takes any key. format.ts · version.ts Relative times, and the build's own version. The persistent frame src/lib/chrome/ holds the title bar, toolbar, nav rail, repository tabs, status strip and resize edges. The window is created with decorations: false , so the platform draws no title bar and Spagitty draws its own — which is also why the title bar is the drag handle and the resize edges are a component. Three things are mounted once, by the shell Dialog (every confirmation), Notice (every result) and the command log drawer. An operation started on the graph can finish after the user has navigated away, and a dialog owned by a screen would take the question with it. The shared UI kit ui/Menu.svelte Every right-click menu in the application is this component with a different list. ui/DialogHost · dialog.svelte.ts Every confirmation. ui/NoticeToast · notice.svelte.ts Every result. ui/Splitter.svelte Every resize handle. It measures the panel beside it rather than the window — the window's edge is the right reference only for the rail. ui/columns.svelte.ts A table's columns: which are shown, in what order, how wide — per repository. Extracted from the graph when the Branches screen needed the same thing. ui/liquidGlass.ts · liquidGlassMaps.ts The refraction. The arithmetic is pure and tested without a window; the measuring half does nothing at all when there is no lens to filter — which is every component test. ui/Icon.svelte · icons.ts The icon set as data. ui/BrandMark · RefChip · Chip · Btn The small shared pieces. ui/ScreenStub.svelte Rendered by no route any more. It stays because it is how the next unbuilt screen says what it will be rather than pretending to be it — a half-built screen that looks real is harder to read than an honest empty one. The command palette src/lib/palette/ is a registry, not a list . commands.ts contributes the shell's own commands — navigation, the graph's view controls, appearance, and the two repository-wide git verbs — and a feature contributes its own next to itself, so no single file has to import every feature in order to name it. It is the one place that picks its key notation from the platform at runtime, because macOS is a build target and printing Ctrl+ on a machine with no such key would be wrong. Notable stores The graph store Rows live in a plain array, not in $state . A repository with 200,000 commits would mean 200,000 deeply-proxied objects, and every batch would pay to re-wrap them. Instead the array is untracked and a version counter is the reactive signal: appending a batch is O(batch), and consumers re-read what they need. Nothing in the store holds a DOM node — the row list is virtualised and the lanes are drawn on canvas. Around it: graph/lanes.ts Lane drawing. One canvas covers the lane column for the visible window only. graph/portrait.ts The author portrait as a description, rendered two ways — canvas for the node, CSS gradients for the Author column — so a person has one face on screen. graph/visibility.svelte.ts Hide, solo, smart visibility, pin-to-left. Each resolves to a root set for a fresh walk. graph/selection.svelte.ts A second selection, deliberately: the detail panel shows exactly one row, and the operations that act on several need their own. graph/overlay.svelte.ts The two things on the graph that are not commits — the work-in-progress node and the stashes. graph/actions.ts What the menus actually do. Kept apart from the menus that describe them, because the sentence shown before a reset --hard is as much of the feature as the reset. The farm store Driven by events rather than a poll: a farm changes when an agent says something, which is at a model's pace and on no schedule. The backend emits, the store applies, and the screen is a function of the store. A snapshot is refetched

d: Every Tauri command and every event that crosses between the webview and the backend, grouped by what it is for.
b: How it is built IPC reference Every Tauri command and every event that crosses between the webview and the backend. All of them are reached from exactly one module on the frontend — src/lib/api.ts , plus src/lib/farm/api.ts for the farm — so a rename here is a one-file change there. Conventions Types crossing the boundary derive Serialize with #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] and are mirrored by hand in src/lib/types.ts . Errors cross as plain strings — Error 's Display text is user-facing, and screens show it directly rather than substituting a message of their own. The session and the walk Command Does open_repo Opens a repository, builds the ref index, computes the cheap counts, spawns a graph worker and a watcher. Returns { info, counts, token } . close_repo Tears down the walk and the watcher. graph_request Asks the worker for the next n rows. The worker walks nothing until asked. graph_restart Starts a fresh walk. The old one's rows are dropped by token rather than cancelled. graph_visibility Hide, solo, smart visibility and pin-to-left — resolved to a root set for a fresh walk, never a client-side filter. snapshot The repository's current state in one read: HEAD, counts, freshness. metrics The Rust side's structural constants, fetched at boot so the two copies of the row pitch can be compared. launch_path The path the binary was started with, if any. Reading Command Does commit_detail The message and the people for one commit. commit_diff A commit's file list and totals — step one of the Diff screen's two-step load. file_diff One file's hunks, fetched as it is selected and cached by path. binary_file_diff A size delta and a MIME type, for a file that has no lines. working_copy The status walk: staged, unstaged, untracked. working_diff · binary_working_diff The same two, for uncommitted work. head_message The current HEAD's message — what an amend starts from. branches Every branch with its drift, upstream and merged state. stashes The stash list, read from refs/stash 's reflog. blame Line attribution for a file. The one read that goes through the git binary. file_history A file's commits, following renames. conflicts · conflict_sides · conflict_regions What is conflicted, the three index stages of one path, and the marker regions inside it. reflog · reflog_refs Where a ref has been, and which refs have a reflog at all. tags Annotated and lightweight, told apart. worktrees · submodules The linked working trees, and the submodules with their status. remotes The remotes this repository knows about. search_start · search_stop Start a filtered walk on its own thread; starting one cancels the one before. external_tools_config Which diff and merge tools are installed, and what git is configured to use. recent_repos The repositories the user has opened. Nothing scans the filesystem. Writing The working copy Command Does stage · unstage By path. stage_hunk · unstage_hunk By hunk, through a generated patch. discard · discard_hunk The only writes here that can lose work, and the only ones behind a confirmation. commit Commits the index, through git , so hooks and signing behave exactly as they would in a terminal. History Command Does reset Soft, mixed or hard — named by effect at the call site rather than by flag. revert · cherry_pick Single or over a selection. integrate Merge, rebase or fast-forward as one verb with a mode, which is what the drag gesture on the graph produces. rebase_onto A branch onto another. rebase_todo · rebase_preview The generated plan, and the fold of it. Neither starts anything. rebase_run · rebase_progress Execution on a worker, with progress read from git's state counters. rebase_continue · rebase_skip · rebase_abort The three ways out of a stopped rebase. checkout · checkout_detached Through git switch for a branch, which only ever changes branch. create_branch · rename_branch · delete_branch Names validated by git, not by a second implementation of check-ref-format . create_tag · delete_tag From the graph's context menu. tag_create · tag_delete · tag_retag From the Tags screen, which also rewrites an annotated message. stash_push · stash_action Push, and then pop / apply / drop as one action with a mode. Conflicts Command Does conflict_take Take a whole side. conflict_resolve_region Take one marker region. conflict_write Write what was typed into the merged pane. conflict_resolve Mark a path resolved — an explicit git add , so the index says what the screen says. conflict_continue · conflict_abort The two ways out of the operation itself. Remotes, worktrees, submodules, tools Commands Does remote_add · remote_rename · remote_remove · remote_set_url Each through git remote rather than a config edit, so git's own bookkeeping stays correct. worktree_add · worktree_remove · worktree_lock · worktree_unlock · worktree_prune The linked working tree lifecycle. submodule_update · submodule_sync · submodule_deinit Recursive init and update, URL sync, and deinit. set_external_tool · launch_external_diff · launch_external_merge Writes git's own diff.tool / merge.tool , and launches them. Network Command Does fetch · push · pull On a worker, watched while they run. network_release tears one down. clone_plan Where a URL and a folder say the clone will land, and everything wrong with that — computed as the user types, without the network. clone_start · clone_release The one spawn that does not wait. Cancelling removes only what the clone created. check_update Whether there is a newer Spagitty. A check, not an updater. The forge Command Does forge_repo Which host, owner and repository the open repository belongs to. forge_accounts · forge_connect · forge_disconnect Connected accounts. The token goes to the OS keychain; only a host and a login are stored. pull_requests The list — one GraphQL request per refresh. create_pull_request Opens one from the current branch. pull_request_files · pull_request_commits · commit_files The review workspace's three lists. pull_request_comm

h.t: The one test that crosses the language boundary
What is tested away from the markup
Tests that hold a rule rather than a behaviour
The fixture repository for manual sweeps

b: How we work Testing What is checked, how, and what is deliberately not. Anything that reads a repository is tested against a real one; anything pure is tested as a table; and the parts that need a window say so rather than pretending a mock proved something. Headless cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --workspace bun run check # svelte-kit sync && svelte-check bun run test # vitest, run through bun bun run coverage # vitest with the coverage floor enforced Coverage of first-party code is measured on both sides and both must clear their floor: cargo llvm-cov --workspace \ --ignore-filename-regex '(fixture|testing)\.rs' --summary-only bun run coverage Side Floor Scope Rust 70% lines The workspace, with fixture.rs excluded — it is test scaffolding, and counting a helper every test exercises would lift the figure without any product code being tested. Frontend 65% branches src/lib/** . src/testing/** is excluded for the same reason, and src/routes/** because those files are the screens' shells and their logic lives in src/lib . They are not the same number, and neither is a line count for the whole tree. Each floor is defined once — in the workflow for Rust, in vite.config.ts for the frontend — so bun run coverage fails locally for exactly the reason it would fail in CI. Fixtures in the Rust tests crates/spagitty-core/src/fixture.rs builds real repositories with the git binary — not with gix , because a fixture built by the library under test would agree with it by construction. Fixture Is Fixture::empty() An initialised repository with no commits. Fixture::woven() The standard history — a merge, a merged branch and an unmerged one, tags of both kinds, stashes — with a clean working copy. Fixture::dirty() The same, with work in progress. Each lives in a temporary directory that is removed with it. Fixtures in the Tauri layer src-tauri tests the graph worker, the watcher's debounce and the session against a real repository too. Two things make that possible: Everything in src-tauri that touches the application is generic over R: tauri::Runtime , so tauri::test::mock_app can supply an AppHandle<MockRuntime> . spagitty-core 's fixtures are public behind a fixture feature, which src-tauri enables as a dev-dependency — one fixture builder for the workspace rather than two things building repositories with the git binary. Nothing enables it outside tests, so a release build carries neither the fixtures nor tempfile . src-tauri/src/testing.rs holds what an event test needs beyond that: a mock application managing the real state, an Emitted<T> collector with at_least(n) and no_more_than(n) , and finishes_promptly , which puts a deadline on a drop. That last one matters — dropping a worker joins its thread, so a worker that ignored its shutdown would hang the runner rather than fail. It also points HOME and the platform's other configuration variables at a temporary directory, once for the whole test binary: open_repo writes to the recent-repositories list, and a test run must not add rows to the list of repositories you have opened. The one test that crosses the language boundary ROW_PITCH exists twice: in src/lib/metrics.ts , which is the source of truth, and in crates/spagitty-core/src/graph.rs , which describes lane elbows in row units and so needs the same number. Two copies of a constant in two languages drift — and they did. The geometry moved on one side while doc comments on both sides claimed a test was holding them together. There was no such test. graph::tests::row_pitch_matches_the_frontend is that test now. It resolves the TypeScript file from CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR , reads the export const ROW_PITCH declaration out of it, and asserts it against the crate's constant — failing with both values named so the message says which side moved. It is the only test that reads another language's source, and it earns that by being about the only constant duplicated across the boundary. Anything else needing to cross should go through the existing IPC types. The frontend Components are mounted for real against happy-dom . The helpers live in src/testing/ : mount.ts renders a component and returns query handles, and there are reactive stand-ins for the two stores the chrome reads. The stand-ins hold real state A stub built from ordinary properties renders once and never updates, so every test about a change would pass by rendering the initial value. What is tested away from the markup Wherever the interesting decision is a pure function, it lives beside the component and is tested as a table: the lane fold, the split-view pairing, the syntax tokeniser, the achievement engine, the farm's scheduler and router, the settings screen's sentences about where a value came from, the divergence bar's geometry, and the glass maps' arithmetic. Tests that hold a rule rather than a behaviour Test Fails if Themes Any of the sixteen palettes drops below 4.5:1 for ordinary text or 3:1 for secondary text, the accent or a lane colour — computed with translucent tokens composited over what shows through them. Or if two families ever share an accent hue. Settings sections A chip is added without an explicit branch behind it. The screen used to have an {:else} catch-all, and one chip silently drew the wrong section for weeks. Pull requests A host's name appears anywhere in the screen, or more than one HTTP client exists, or one is declared outside spagitty-core , or it is reachable from more than one file. Conflicts Reading a conflicted repository modifies the index or leaves a lock behind. All repositories Reading a repository card modifies that repository's index. Interactive rebase The generated todo list disagrees with git rev-list --reverse --no-merges . The working record The index under agile/ and the tree disagree — a missing row, a row with no document, a status that does not match the item, or a cited identifier that resolves to nothing.
