d: Six ordered gates, the coverage floor, the three release lanes, and when a merge publishes.

h.t: Every lane builds all three platforms
Release notes come from the changelog

b: How we work CI/CD & releases The pipeline is a sequence of gates in a fixed order. A gate that fails stops the pipeline; nothing downstream runs. Cheapest and most certain first, so an obvious failure never burns a full three-platform build. The gates # Gate Runs Proves 0 Scope A diff of the push or pull request against the previous tip Whether the change ships in the application. Gates 5 and 6 read this; documentation alone is not a release. 1 License cargo deny check licenses bans sources , a licence check over the JS production tree, plus a check that the licence files and both manifests still say GPL-3.0-or-later Every dependency's licence is identified and permitted, and nothing conflicts with shipping under GPL-3. 2 Code quality cargo fmt --all --check , cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings , bun run check , plus the brand and icon generators in --check mode Formatting, lints and types across both languages, and no drift between the brand generators and the committed art. 3 Tests and coverage cargo llvm-cov --workspace --fail-under-lines 70 , bun run coverage The suite passes and first-party coverage holds its floor: 70% for Rust, 65% branches for the frontend. 4 Security cargo deny check advisories , bun audit --audit-level=high , gitleaks over the diff No known-vulnerable dependency at high or above, and no secret in the change. 5 Build bun run tauri build on Linux, macOS and Windows — main, shipping changes only The release build works on every target, not only the one the author uses. 6 Release Tag, artifacts, and notes read from CHANGELOG.md — main, shipping changes only The build is published, carries its changelog section as notes, and is traceable to a commit. What runs where Branch What happens main Gates 1 to 4 on every push. Gates 5 and 6 run only when the change ships — something under src/ , src-tauri/ , crates/ , or a version, lockfile or frontend config the built application depends on. Passing gate 6 publishes the release. A README, docs, working-record or brand-collateral edit is not a publish: those land without rebuilding three platforms or tagging, and ride the next version. The scope job makes that call. dev Gates 1 to 4, automatically, then the pipeline stops. Building and publishing an alpha from dev is a manual action: run the prerelease workflow and give it an alpha number. It produces vX.Y.Z-alpha.N , which is never a release of main . Pull requests Gates 1 to 4, into either branch. Since a pull request is the only path into a protected branch, that is where the results are read. Every lane builds all three platforms Gate 5 and the prerelease workflow each run on Linux, macOS and Windows runners; the draft workflow builds Linux, Windows, and macOS on two runners — Apple silicon and Intel — since a build made on one does not run on the other. Gate 5's macOS build is Apple silicon only, so a published release currently has no Intel Mac download. That is recorded as an open question rather than fixed unwatched on the blocking release path. Nothing is signed There is no Apple Developer account and no code-signing certificate in this project, so macOS Gatekeeper refuses a downloaded build on a double-click and Windows SmartScreen warns. The draft lane's release notes carry the one step a Mac user needs. Adding real signing is a change to gate 5 and the draft lane together, not to one of them. The rules Gates are blocking, not advisory. A red gate is fixed, not bypassed. continue-on-error is not used to get a merge through, and neither is a re-run until it passes. An advisory that cannot be fixed is recorded, not silenced. The [advisories] ignore list carries accepted risk by advisory id , each with its crate and its reason, so anything not listed still fails gate 4. That is the line between recording a risk and switching the gate off, and only the first is allowed. A blanket setting — unmaintained = "warn" , or dropping the check — is the second wearing different clothes. Sixteen entries are listed today, all unmaintained , none a vulnerability, and eleven of them the GTK3 bindings Tauri links against on Linux with no upgrade available. They are deleted when Tauri moves to GTK4. The order is fixed. A new check joins an existing gate or becomes a new one in the right place — it does not get bolted onto whichever job is convenient. The coverage floor is defined once per language , and the two are not the same number. Tags are never moved. Gate 6 refuses to publish over a tag that already exists and tells you to bump the version instead. Release notes come from the changelog A version's section in CHANGELOG.md becomes that version's release notes verbatim . Gate 6 reads it and refuses to release without one, so a changelog entry is written into ## [Unreleased] in the same change as the work it describes rather than reconstructed afterwards from commit messages. The format follows Keep a Changelog ; versions follow Semantic Versioning . Spagitty is at 0.x : the surface is not stable, MINOR may break, PATCH stays backward-compatible. The three release lanes Lane Triggered by Produces Release A shipping merge into main vX.Y.Z , tagged, with installers for three platforms and the changelog section as notes. Prerelease Run by hand from dev , given an alpha number vX.Y.Z-alpha.N . Never a release of main . Draft Run by hand A draft release, including an Intel macOS build, for checking artifacts before they are public. Running the gates locally Gates 1 to 3 are what a change is checked against before it is committed. bun install --frozen-lockfile # the dependencies, locked cargo deny check licenses bans sources # gate 1 cargo fmt --all --check # gate 2 cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings bun run check python3 tools/make-icons.py --check # gate 2 — brand drift python3 tools/make-brand.py --check cargo llvm-cov --workspace \ --ignore-filename-regex '(fixture|testing)\.rs' --summary-only bun run coverage # gate 3 cargo deny check advisorie

h.t: Status has five words, and only five

b: How we work How we work The product code is one half of this repository. The other half is the working record — why a change existed, what was verified, and what broke along the way — kept in the repository rather than in someone's head. The working record agile/ items/ work items: features, tasks, bugs plans/ one implementation plan per work item testing/ test plans per work item — automated and manual sweep roadmap.md the order the outstanding work is meant to be taken in Identifiers are FEAT-### , TASK-### and BUG-### , assigned in sequence and never reused. The identifier is the join key: an item's four documents are agile/items/FEAT-004-branches.md agile/plans/FEAT-004-plan.md agile/testing/FEAT-004-automated.md agile/testing/FEAT-004-sweep.md and its branch is feature/FEAT-004-branches . Backlog items — recorded but not started — carry an item document only. Their plan and testing documents are written when the work begins, since a plan written before the work is a guess rather than a record. Status has five words, and only five Word Means Done Built and merged. Fixed A bug, fixed and merged. Partial Some of it is built and merged and some is not. The item says which. Open Being worked on now. Backlog Recorded, not started. Item document only. Partial exists because the record had no word for it and used Backlog instead — which sent readers off to write code that was already there. The index is checked by a test tools/record.test.ts runs in the ordinary suite and fails if the index and the tree disagree: a missing row, a row with no document, a status that does not match the item, a cited identifier that resolves to nothing, or a built item whose missing documents are not recorded. Drift is a test failure rather than an audit. Branching Git Flow, with the work item in the branch name. Branch For main Protected. A shipping merge here publishes a release. dev Protected. Gates 1–4 run; alphas are cut from it by hand. feature/FEAT-###-… A new capability. task/TASK-###-… Work that is not a user-visible feature — tooling, records, refactors. bugfix/BUG-###-… A defect. hotfix/… · release/… Urgent fixes, and release preparation. A pull request is the only path into a protected branch. Commits are signed off, and a changelog entry goes under ## [Unreleased] in the same change as the work. The standing rules The binding rules are an amendments book shared across the author's projects and kept outside this repository, so the rules are edited once rather than copied per project. docs/AMENDMENTS.md is a pointer to it and says so explicitly — it is not a second copy, and a summary does not replace the book. The ones that show up most in this repository, in effect: The working record is required. Every change has an item, and the item's status there is authoritative. A document that names a path which no longer exists is a defect , and has to be verified rather than trusted. That rule was applied to the pointer file itself, which for a while named a directory that did not exist on any machine — so the one thing it was for, telling a newcomer where the rules are, it did not do. A pull request is the only path into a protected branch. A release's notes are its changelog section , written with the work rather than generated afterwards. How a change is written An item , with what it is for and how it will be known to be done. A plan , written when the work starts. The change , on a branch named after the item, with the documentation it affects updated in the same commit — a section describing something that no longer exists is a defect. Tests , and a changelog entry under Unreleased . Gates 1 to 3 locally , then a pull request, where gates 1 to 4 are read. A sweep document , filled in with results rather than intentions. Reasoning lives next to the code Module headers in this repository carry the why , not a restatement of the signature. That is a deliberate convention, and it is why the crate references on this wiki can be as specific as they are: the reasoning was already written down, in the file it belongs to. “A search is the same revision walk the graph does, with a predicate and without lanes. It is not a second traversal of history.” Where a decision was reversed , both halves stay — the original reasoning and what turned out to be wrong with it. The Linux rendering path is the clearest example: a workaround that fixed a blank window on some hosts cost every other host the GPU path, and the header now says both things. Defects, kept rather than tidied away The record includes what broke. Not as a confession — as the useful half. A few that shaped the code: A Settings chip that opened the wrong section , because eight chips fed seven branches and an {:else} catch-all hid the miss. The catch-all is gone and a test now fails if a chip is added without a branch. An External Tools section themed against CSS tokens that did not exist , so every palette but one fell through to a hard-coded dark fallback — and nothing failed, because the CSS was valid. A release lane that tagged a version and then could not attach its assets , because a bundle tree was uploaded whole and one icon appeared twice. A release that halted rather than broke : the runner had no git identity, so git tag -a refused with fatal: empty ident name , nothing was tagged and nothing was published. The fix set the bot identity and, with it, moved the notes off generated text and onto the changelog. A coverage floor the delight layer briefly dropped under , recovered by mounting the surfaces that had been left at 0% branches. Eight themes wearing one accent , because “the brand runs through the UI” was applied literally. Each family accents in its own hue now, and a test fails if two ever share one. A rail whose loudest pixel was a filled button offering to replace the repository you were working in — above every screen, wanted approximately never. A lens that wiped the window. h.t: Rules the wording has to keep

b: How we work Brand & identity The mark, the wordmark, the palette, the words we lead with, and the rules that keep them consistent. Every asset is generated deterministically from one vector source, and a gate rejects a change where the generators and the committed art disagree. The words we lead with These are the approved forms. They exist because a product describes itself the same way everywhere or it does not have a description at all. Use Text Tagline Untangle the work — yours, and your agents'. Product description Spagitty, your gateway to a Git-managed agent farm. One-line descriptor A local-first desktop Git client for repositories where people and coding agents commit side by side. Short descriptor A desktop Git client built for the review that follows fast work. Category Desktop Git client — gateway to a Git-managed agent farm. Rules the wording has to keep Never “AI-powered”. Nothing in Spagitty is a model. Saying otherwise trades away the one thing a local-first tool has, which is that you can tell what it is doing. The possessive is on the agents, not the user. “yours, and your agents'” — plural possessive, apostrophe after the s. It is the most commonly mistyped part of the tagline. The em dash is an em dash , not a hyphen, and the tagline ends in a full stop. It is a sentence. Keep the metaphor literal. Tangled and straightened, pasta and strands. Do not extend it into cooking, chefs or kitchens in product copy — that register belongs to the delight layer, where it is deliberately a joke, and mixing the two makes the serious claims read as jokes too. The name and the metaphor Spagitty — spa-gi-ty — is a deliberate portmanteau of spaghetti and Git . A complex repository without clear lane graphs, divergence tracking and structured review trails quickly becomes a messy plate of tangled pasta. The mission is to untangle the pasta bowl into clear, straight strands of intent. Tone of voice Honest and direct. We state what actions do, without patronising marketing speak or artificial excitement. Crafted and precise. Geometry is deliberate, flat, and legible down to a 16-pixel icon. Respectful of the machine. Zero bloat, instant response, local-first offline operation. The mark The amber plate ( #EEB04D ) — a warm rounded ground, the plate the strands lie on. Four dark strands ( #454447 ) — beginning tangled and overlapping at the top and resolving into straight, parallel paths flowing downward. The master source is assets/brand/mark.svg on a 912 × 953 viewBox. Flat, and non-destructive The mark contains zero gradients, drop shadows, inner bevels or outlines. And the vector path data is permanent: it is never manually redrawn or replaced by an algorithmic approximation. Clearspace A mandatory boundary of 1× , where × is 15% of the mark's total height, surrounds the mark and the lockup on all four sides. No text, icon, border or secondary element may intrude into it. The wordmark and the lockup Lowercase spagitty , set in Inter at weight 660 with +0.045em tracking. Strictly lowercase. The lockup puts the mark on the left and the wordmark on the right along a shared optical centreline, with a gap of about 20% of the mark's height. There are two ink variants — light text for dark backgrounds, dark charcoal for light ones — because a single lockup cannot be legible on both. The palette Brand colours --brand-amber #EEB04D rgb(238,176,77) the plate --brand-ink #454447 rgb(69,68,71) the strands --brand-ink-dark #CDD6F4 ink on dark surfaces The interactive accent adapts Surface Value Contrast Used for Dark themes #EEB04D > 7.2:1 (AAA) Focus rings, primary buttons, active tabs, selected branch chips Light themes #976317 4.6:1 (AA) The darkened amber, for readable links, active states and borders In the application itself each palette family goes further and accents in its own hue — see themes & appearance . The brand amber remains the brand's colour; it is not imposed on every theme. Lane and semantic colours --lane-1 #89B4FA blue --lane-2 #A6E3A1 green · added --lane-3 #F9E2AF yellow --lane-4 #CBA6F7 mauve --lane-5 #F38BA8 pink · danger · deleted Generated assets Everything below is produced from mark.svg by tools/make-icons.py and tools/make-brand.py . The derived files are never hand-edited. Target Size Treatment Master mark 512 × 512 Amber plate and strands. Hero banner 1600 × 400 Mark and wordmark on one centreline, with the approved tagline under. App icons 16² to 1024² High-DPI set with @2x assets. Windows icon Multi-size .ico 16, 32, 48, 64, 128 and 256 px frames. macOS icon Multi-size .icns Apple's standard bundle. macOS menu bar 18 × 18 ( @2x 36²) Pure alpha monochrome template — strands only , no plate, per Apple's guidelines. System tray 22 × 22 ( @2x 44²) White strands for dark taskbars, charcoal for light ones. Favicon Multi-size .ico Browser tab icon. Determinism is a gate Gate 2 in CI runs both generators in --check mode and rejects a change whose asset bytes have drifted. Regenerate collateral with the scripts; never hand-edit a derived PNG. Binding rules Never use the Git logo or Git orange ( #F05133 ). Spagitty is an independent client and is not affiliated with the Git project. Never redraw or approximate the mark. No procedural noodles, no bezier approximations, no CSS pseudo-element icons. Reference the source or a generated asset. Never add gradients or drop shadows to brand assets. All branding is strictly flat. Always use theme-aware CSS variables — var(--accent) , var(--brand-amber) — never a raw hex in a component style where light-mode adaptability is required. Enforce deterministic generation. Run the generators whenever collateral changes. Preserve the menu-bar template rules. macOS menu-bar and tray icons carry the four strands and no plate. Licensing The brand artwork and the code are under GPL-3.0-or-later . The Inter typeface is under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 , bundled with its licence text. h.t: Design rules that are not negotiable

b: How we work Contributing Bug reports and pull requests are welcome. This page is the short version; the authoritative text is CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository. The repository Issues CONTRIBUTING.md Read these first Architecture — the three layers and the rules that hold their seams. How we work — the working record, and why a change starts with an item. Testing — what is checked and how. CI/CD & releases — the gates your change has to clear. Licence of contributions Spagitty is GPL-3.0-or-later . By contributing you agree that your contribution is licensed under GPL-3.0-or-later. There is no CLA and no copyright assignment — you keep the copyright to your work. Every new source file gets an SPDX header as its first line: // SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-or-later <!-- Rust, TypeScript --> <!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-or-later --> <!-- Svelte, Markdown --> Developer Certificate of Origin We use the DCO rather than a CLA. Sign off every commit: git commit -s That appends Signed-off-by: Your Name <you@example.com> . The name and email must be real and must match the commit author. Branch and commit Every branch carries a work item id from agile/ : feature/FEAT-###-… , task/TASK-###-… , bugfix/BUG-###-… . If your change does not have an item yet, open one — it is a short document, and it is what makes the record readable a year later. A pull request is the only path into main or dev . A changelog entry goes under ## [Unreleased] in the same change as the work. Gate 6 reads that file for release notes and refuses to release without a section. Update the documentation your change affects, in the same commit. A section describing something that no longer exists is a defect. Before you push cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --workspace bun run check bun run coverage The full local gate sequence, including licences and advisories, is on CI/CD & releases . Dependencies Check the licence before adding one. Acceptable: MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC, MPL-2.0, LGPL, GPL-2.0-with-linking-exception, CC0, OFL (fonts). Not acceptable: proprietary, SSPL, BSL, or any “source available” non-free licence. Apache-2.0-only code must not be linked into GPL-2.0-only code. A new dependency has to show up in the generated third-party licence list, and it has to be justified in the change that adds it. Design rules that are not negotiable These come from the design handoff and hold across every screen. Standard git terminology only. fetch, push, stage, hunk, stash@{n} , pick/squash/reword/drop, ours/theirs. No invented vocabulary, no friendly renaming of git concepts. Structural numbers are shared constants, never literals. The commit row pitch, the rail width, the detail panel width and the lane pitch each have exactly one definition. If you find yourself typing 26 , use the constant. Never block on walking the whole history. The graph streams in windows and paints progressively. Destructive actions are reversible. Rebase previews before executing; conflict resolution writes nothing until finished; Undo maps to a reflog restore. Nothing leaves the machine. Repositories are read straight from disk; credentials go in the OS keychain. Never use the Git logo or Git orange. See brand & identity . Code style Rust: cargo fmt and cargo clippy clean. Frontend: bun run check clean. Do not reimplement what shell.rs should shell out to git for — interactive rebase execution, hooks, LFS, submodule recursion, credential helpers. If you need a new one of those, add it there with a comment explaining why gix is not the right tool, and extend the boundary table in the same change. Do not reformat files you are not otherwise changing. A diff that is 90% whitespace is a diff nobody can review. Write the why in the module header. A comment restating the signature is noise; the reasoning behind a choice is the thing that cannot be recovered from the code. Reporting a bug Useful reports say: Which screen, by its code if you know it ( 1A , 1H , …). Your platform and Spagitty version — Settings → License has both, along with the exact commit the build came from. What you did, what happened, and what you expected instead. If it involves a git operation, what Show the git command behind each action recorded. That drawer shows the actual argv, not a reconstruction. For a suspected vulnerability, describe the class of problem rather than posting a working exploit.

d: Every version of Spagitty and what shipped in it, newest first.
b: How we work Release history Every version of Spagitty and what shipped in it, newest first. The full text is in CHANGELOG.md , which is also what gate 6 reads to produce a release's notes — a version's section becomes those notes verbatim. Latest release Full changelog Versioning Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 , and Spagitty is at 0.x : the surface is not yet stable, MINOR may break, PATCH stays backward-compatible. The format follows Keep a Changelog . 0.5.1 — 6 September 2026 A reliability pass over the farm's edges, plus a development-mode styling fix. Automatic merges got stricter. They now require passing checks and a successful independent review of the work actually committed , plus merge permission. Tasks keep their intended destination, and competing farm merges serialise rather than racing. Verification output is drained continuously with bounded retention, and stopping a check or reaching its deadline terminates its whole process tree. One completion watcher per run , review runs included, so a late result stays attached to the attempt that produced it. Running agents and planners stay cancellable while background threads wait on them; Windows agent descendants are contained in a job before execution starts. Development window sizing stays intact when a component stylesheet request arrives before its JavaScript. Frontend routes are measured in coverage, and descendant termination is checked on all three platforms before a release. 0.5.0 — 5 September 2026 The farm could run a plan but there was almost no way to watch it run. This is that release: a ring rather than a count, a chip for every working agent, a log you can read and filter, a queue that says why a task is waiting, and a task too big for one agent that can be cut into smaller ones. Added The Farm screen is worth watching. 3 / 7 done becomes a ring — finished fills it, running is a brighter arc at its leading edge, blocked colours the rest — so a farm that is working looks different from one that stopped at the same count. One chip per working agent says who is on what and for how long. A run that has gone quiet says so. After six minutes without a word the chip and the row say how long it has been silent and the pulse stops. Nothing is stopped for you. Agents earn their badges from the farm. A task taken all the way to Done scores the agent that did it — whether the checks really passed, whether the reviewer approved, how many times it was sent back. Every task says who asked for it. Your own tasks stay unmarked; anything an agent asked for carries one quiet mark, and its panel says which agent and why. A task that is too big can be broken down. The subtasks arrive as a proposed plan under it, and the task becomes a heading that finishes when they do. A plan may hold 24 tasks; a farm may run 8 agents at once; the attempt limit became a setting. A proposed plan is accepted in one action — a band with a checkbox per task, rather than opening each one. A queued task says why it is not running , in the scheduler's own words. The farm's log is a drawer you can read , with Activity and Transcript tabs, following, and Hold. A little motion, where it says something — and nothing at all for a reader who has asked for reduced motion. Changed A long session stops growing. The run history is bounded now; transcripts were always on disk and the drawer can read a task's whole log back from one. Every farm event carries the time it happened , which is what makes a log a log. Watching a farm costs almost nothing. The refresh no longer runs git worktree list and re-parses the whole activity log on the thread that paints the window. 0.4.1-alpha — 3 September 2026 A pass over the palettes and the rail. Four more palette families — Nord, Rosé Pine, Solarized and Everforest, each in light and dark, bringing the set to eight families and sixteen palettes. Every theme now accents in its own hue. They all wore the brand amber, which put one colour on seven palettes built around a different one. A test now fails if two families ever share an accent. The Farm is the rail's first screen , and the Graph follows it. The Graph still owns / . Open repository leaves the rail once a repository is open. It was a filled accent button above every screen offering to replace the repository you were working in. The repository's state moved from the rail's foot to the status strip — one line, in two groups, rather than four stacked lines duplicating the rail's own badges. The Farm's first screen is a starter page , not an empty state: what a farm is, the loop in four steps, a goal field, and three readiness rows. 0.4.0-alpha — 3 September 2026 The agent farm. The agent farm. Spagitty runs and shepherds coding agents instead of only reading what they did. A new crates/spagitty-farm is the control plane and nothing else — every git operation still goes through spagitty-core . Inside it: the domain model, one adapter per provider, a branch and worktree per task with path-level lease locks, a deterministic verifier, a peer-review router, a dependency-DAG scheduler, and local persistence. The first release to carry its pre-release suffix in the manifest. 0.3.0 — 2 September 2026 Ten features, and four defects found on the way. Added Worktrees management — view, add, switch, lock, unlock, remove and prune linked working trees. File history and interactive blame — screen 1O, with rename following and a line-by-line gutter. Diff syntax highlighting — grammar-based, mapped onto the theme's own palette tokens. Image and binary diffs — side-by-side, swipe and onion-skin comparison; size deltas for binaries. Diff content search — search inside added and removed patch lines. Submodules management — status, recursive init and update, sync, deinit. External diff and merge tools — discovery and launch, through git's own configuration keys. Multi-identity profiles — named author identities, applied locally or globally. Extended forge integration and in-app PR creation — GitLab

d: The vocabulary this wiki uses — Spagitty's own terms and the git ones it leans on.

h.t: Git terms, as Spagitty uses them

b: How we work Glossary The vocabulary this wiki uses. Spagitty's own terms first, then the git ones it leans on — because the rule in the interface is standard git terminology only, and that only helps if the terms are defined somewhere. Spagitty's own terms Agent A coding assistant with a command line, installed on your machine — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Oh My Pi, or one you configure yourself. Spagitty runs agents; it does not contain them. Agent farm A goal, the tasks it was cut into, and the agents working them in parallel. See the agent farm . Autonomy level Where you stand in the loop, from Manual (nothing runs by itself) to Unattended . Five settings, each a sentence rather than a slider. Badge An achievement in the delight layer, earned per repository and per actor. Never awarded for time spent in the application. The bed The lane column's background, laid out once at the full height of the table underneath the rows — what a repository shorter than the window needs so the column does not simply end at the last commit. Delight layer Badges, titles, cards and sounds. Deliberately a sink: git actions push events into it and it pushes nothing back. Divergence bar The two-sided bar on the Branches screen showing ahead and behind, scaled against the widest drift on screen. It replaced ↑2 ↓3 , which read worst in exactly the case that matters. First-pass rate How often an agent's work passed verification and review without being sent back. The only thing agents are ranked by — volume ranks whoever was given the most work. Forge A repository host: GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket Cloud. Kept host-agnostic in the interface, with a test that fails if a host's name appears in a screen. Glass / the lens The frosted, refracting chrome. The filter is applied to the application underneath a pane rather than to the pane itself, because the usual web technique renders nothing on WebKitGTK. Handoff The structured thing an agent returns at the end of a run — status, a test report, proposed tasks — alongside its prose. Hold A control in the farm's log drawer that freezes the list so a line can be read while it is still arriving, and counts what arrived meanwhile. Distinct from following , which is just where the scrollbar is. Lease A path-level claim a task holds while it runs. Worktrees stop two agents corrupting each other's files; leases stop two of them editing the same path. Portrait The author avatar drawn on a commit node, generated from the email address and never fetched — so it is the same on every machine, and an offline repository looks no different from an online one. Root set What a visibility control resolves to: the tips a fresh walk starts from. Never a filter over rows already drawn, which would leave lanes drawing edges between commits that are not parent and child. Screen code The short handle for a screen — 1A , 1H , 1Q — so it can be named in one token. See the screen reference . Sweep A manual test pass against the fixture repository, recorded as filled-in results in the work item's own document. Task The farm's unit of work: machine-readable, with a kind, dependencies, expected paths and its own verification commands. Verification Running the repository's own commands against an agent's work, in that task's worktree. The gate between “the agent says it is done” and “it is done”. Work item A FEAT-### , TASK-### or BUG-### under agile/ , with its plan and test documents. The join key between a branch, a commit and the record. Working record The agile/ directory as a whole — why a change existed, what was verified, and what broke along the way. Git terms, as Spagitty uses them Ahead / behind How many commits a branch has that its upstream does not, and vice versa. Counted against the remote-tracking ref on disk , so the numbers are as old as the last fetch — and Spagitty says how old rather than implying they are live. Annotated tag A tag that is its own object and can carry a message. A lightweight tag is just a ref. The difference decides whether a message can exist at all, so the two are told apart throughout. Blame Which commit last touched each line of a file. Cherry-pick Applying one commit's change onto another branch, producing a new commit. Detached HEAD HEAD pointing at a commit rather than a branch. Reachable deliberately from the graph, and recoverable through the reflog. Fast-forward Moving a branch pointer forward when there is nothing to merge, because the target already contains it. Hunk A contiguous block of changed lines in a diff, with its context. Spagitty stages, unstages and discards by hunk as well as by file. Index (the staging area) What the next commit will contain. During a conflict it holds all three versions of a file — stage 1 the base, stage 2 ours, stage 3 theirs — which is the whole data model of the Conflicts screen. Lane A vertical column in the commit graph. A branch's line of development as drawn, not as named. Ours / theirs The two sides of a conflict. Which is which depends on the operation, which is why Spagitty reads the operation in progress from the repository's own state rather than inferring it. Reflog Where a ref has been. What answers “what did I just do to this history”, and the way back from almost anything. Rebase (interactive) Replaying a run of commits onto a new base, optionally reordering, squashing, rewording or dropping them along the way. Remote-tracking ref The local record of where a remote branch was at the last fetch. Not the remote itself. Squash Folding a commit into the one above it. b: How we work FAQ Common questions, answered plainly. If the answer is longer than a paragraph it lives on its own page and this points at it. Using it What does Spagitty cost? Nothing. It is free software under the GPL-3.0-or-later, with no paid tier, no account and no service behind it. If you run coding agents through the farm, those agents cost whatever they cost — that is between you and their providers. Which platforms? Linux, macOS and Windows. Every release builds all three. The published macOS build is Apple silicon; the draft lane also produces an Intel one. See install & first run . Why does macOS refuse to open it? Nothing is code-signed — there is no Apple Developer account in this project. Right-click the app, choose Open , then Open again in the dialog. On Windows, choose More info → Run anyway . Adding real signing is tracked, not ignored. Does it need git installed? Yes. Reads are answered in-process with gix , but every operation that writes goes through the git binary — deliberately, so hooks, credential helpers, LFS, submodule recursion and the sequencer all behave exactly as they would in a terminal. See the boundary . Can I open more than one repository? There is a tab strip, and tabs can point at linked worktrees as well as repositories. One repository is open at a time in the backend — opening another tears down the previous walk and watcher — but switching between tabs is what you would expect. Where did my setting go? Behaviour toggles, the repository list and connected accounts live in Spagitty's own configuration directory. The theme, the size dials, column layouts and badge records live in the webview's localStorage , keyed by repository path — because they have to be applied on the first frame, before any command could answer. The full table is on install & first run . Privacy What does Spagitty send? Pull request data to the forge you connected, git's own network operations to your remotes, and an update check when you ask for one. That is the complete list, and it is enumerated on privacy & security . Is there telemetry? No. No analytics, no crash reporting, no usage metrics, no account. There is nowhere for any of it to go — there is no Spagitty server. Where does my forge token live? The OS keychain, and nowhere else. accounts.json holds a host and a login. A token that appears in a clone URL is stripped from the command record before the entry is stored, so it cannot leak through the copy button. How can I check any of that? Two files. Exactly one HTTP client exists in the workspace, declared only in spagitty-core and reachable only from forge/http.rs ; and exactly one module spawns a process, shell.rs . Both are asserted by tests. The webview links no HTTP client at all. The agent farm Does Spagitty include an AI model? No. Nothing here performs inference and nothing ships an API key. The farm runs agents you have installed, as you, with your credentials. Which agents does it support? Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Oh My Pi are detected on PATH out of the box, and anything else with a command line can be added by hand — a configured command with a prompt token, so a new provider is a settings change rather than a release. Can an agent break my working copy? No. Every task runs on its own branch in its own worktree, and nothing an agent does reaches your checkout. Path-level leases stop two agents editing the same file, and deleting a task keeps the commits on its branch. Can an agent merge its own work? Only at the top of the autonomy dial, and even then only with passing checks, a successful review by a different agent of the work actually committed, and merge permission. There is no path in the code from an agent's own report of success to Done . What if nothing is configured to verify the work? The task says so, in those words, when it reaches review. It does not read as verified. “Nothing checked it” is a distinct state from “it passed”. What if an agent goes quiet? After six minutes without a word, the chip and the row say how long it has been silent and the pulse stops. Nothing is killed for you — a model may think for a long time, and killing it throws the work away. What happens if Spagitty crashes mid-farm? The farm is written to disk after every state change, by rename, with an append-only event log. On restart the service reconciles what is on disk against the worktrees that actually exist, and sweep removes what a crashed run left behind. Comparisons How is this different from the Git client I already use? In three ways that matter. It is local-first with no account , and the claim is narrow enough to be checked rather than trusted. It treats agents as first-class actors — credited separately, ranked by first-pass rate, and now run from inside the client. And it is meant to be read : the reasoning behind each decision is in the repository, not in someone's head. What it deliberately does not do is also written down: no dragging commits in the graph, no inline message editing, no manual lane layout, no independent graph zoom. Is it a GitHub client? It is a Git client that can talk to GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud when you connect an account. The Pull requests screen is the only screen whose data comes off the network; everything else reads the disk, and Spagitty works fully offline without any account at all. Is the farm a CI system? No. Verification runs your repository's commands locally, in a task's worktree, as a gate before a merge. It is not a pipeline, it does not run on push, and it replaces nothing you already have. Contributing and licensing Can I use Spagitty commercially? Yes, within the terms of the GPL-3.0-or-later. If you distribute a modified version, the licence requires you to make the corresponding source available under the same terms.
